claim_details.claim: The question of whether humans possess innate knowledge has been debated for centuries, with philosophers and researchers presenting sharply opposing views. On one side, innatists such as Plato, Descartes Leibniz argued that certain knowledge—whether mathematical, linguistic conceptual—is present from birth psychological research has since provided empirical support for this view, showing that the human brain possesses important innate knowledge such as understanding three-dimensional objects and that babies expect objects to persist even when out of sight ; more recently, some researchers argue that humans and many nonhuman animals have an evolved innate capacity to process numbers, suggesting that mathematical perception is innate rather than entirely learned

On the other side, 17th-century philosopher John Locke mounted a rigorous case against innate knowledge, arguing that the mind at birth is a tabula rasa (blank slate) and that all knowledge—even mathematical truths—is derived solely from sensory experience ; Locke further contended that it makes no sense to claim we know something we are not aware of knowing, casting doubt on the very concept of unconscious innate ideas

This enduring debate—between those who see the mind as pre-equipped with certain knowledge and those who view it as entirely shaped by experience—remains unresolved, in part because humans are psychologically biased against accepting that knowledge can be inborn, a phenomenon researchers have termed 'innately antinativist' reasoning

claim_details.claim: Whether pregnant women should follow a vegan diet is a subject of genuine scientific debate. On one hand, several scientific societies—including the U.S. Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics—have issued official position statements favoring well-planned complete plant-based diets during pregnancy, provided they include reliable sources of vitamin B12 and vitamin D ; research suggests such diets can be just as healthy as conventional diets, may reduce the risk of preeclampsia and gestational diabetes appear to carry no greater risk of pregnancy complications than omnivorous diets

On the other hand, Belgium's Royal Academy of Medicine issued a recommendation that pregnant women should not follow a vegan diet, citing unavoidable nutritional shortfalls and potential irreversible harms to the developing brain , a view echoed by some sources cautioning that vegan diets require careful planning to ensure adequate protein, iron, calcium B12 intake

Ultimately, if a pregnant woman chooses a vegan diet, it must be well-planned with fortified foods and supplements she should consult a registered dietitian or healthcare provider to monitor nutrient status throughout pregnancy
